Thrusting upward; moving against the current or with it. Even for those with the eyes of a hawk or a falcon, one household does not know the affairs of another.
Tonight at Mount Mao, I shall set aside my majestic brilliance to meet you all. (He strikes the whisk.
"The hundred and fifth day from winter solstice to cold food festival; twenty-four breezes that herald the flowering season. Again, he cites: Magu asked Linji—
“Regarding the Thousand Hands and Eyes of Great Compassion: which one is the True Eye? Mazu asked. Gu said, “Regarding the Thousand Hands and Eyes of Great Compassion:
which one is the True Eye? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Gu sat down upon the meditation seat. Mazu greeted him, saying, “I hope you are well. Gu hesitated.
Mazu dragged Gu down from the meditation seat, sat back down himself, and Gu immediately went out. The Master said, “It was not for anyone but Ma Gu that this occurred.”
This sufficiently cures the mortal ailment of Linji; yet it was none other than Linji who could perceive the vulnerabilities of Magu.
If this were the true eye, where would there even be room for such things?
Carrying his bowl, he arrived at Ba’en Temple in Jiahe. The assembly requested a small-scale discourse (xiaochan). "Jiahe is a sacred ground, a site of practice for Emperor Shizu;

its scenic splendor fills the eyes, yet even crows cannot fly across it. Within the ten-foot room, flowers rain down everywhere upon the floor; the ice-cold valley gives forth a warm and harmonious air."

The spring breeze flaunts its charms; the Eye of the True Dharma has smashed the sand pot. Who would dare look upon it with a direct eye? This old fellow holds his bowl, overstepping boundaries and encroaching on territory.
Thus, let the guest listen while the host decides. Suddenly, he picks up his staff and says: "What can be done about this traveling staff?
Its branches itch and it leaps about. He strikes once and says: "After the last snow on the mountain plum, before the clouds have yet combed her hair."
Again, [the Master] cited the case of Xuansha asking Jingqing: "Not seeing a single dharma is a great calamity. Tell me, what dharma do you not see?
Jingqing pointed to a pillar and said, "Is it that you do not see this dharma? Xuansha said, "As for the clear water and white rice of Zhejiang, you may eat as much as you like;
as for the Buddha-dharma, you have not even dreamed of it. The Master said: "It is so, yet it is so. It is precisely like shooting an arrow at a target."
The assembly! Their strength is equal and their power is balanced; yet even they cannot avoid celebrating with vegetarian feasts. How will the Jade Couch and Guangxiao Temple see one another?
He lets out a shout and descends from the seat.

At the request of the assembly at Chengtian Temple, I offer these words for a small discourse (xiaocan). The Double Emei Peaks rise so loftily that those who approach can only stare in wonder, finding no way to enter.
The Jade Green Basin is empty yet responds to all things, having no fixed location. Guest and host accord, and lord and subject are harmonious;

the lid fits the box. The mud ox roars at the moon; the wooden horse neighs in the wind. The asura dances the *zhazhi* with graceful movements; the Śūnyatā-deva adds a smile to his face. This is it—this is the realization.
Suddenly, as if drawing forth the weapons and armor of the Three Mysteries and establishing the sovereign and subject of the Five Ranks—how would you respond?
Striking the whisk, he said: "Still grasping the golden whip, he asks the traveler returning home; at this late hour, who walks with him through the Imperial Street?"
Furthermore, during the reign of Emperor Xianzong, Chan Master Dayi of Eagle Lake (E’hu) was summoned to the imperial court.
A Dharma Master asked him, “In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is no dhyāna; dhyāna resides in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Upon what basis is the name ‘dhyāna’ established in this land?

Dayi replied, “Dharma Master, you only know that there is no dhyāna in the realm of desire; you do not know that within the realm of dhyāna, there is no desire. The Dharma Master then asked, “What is dhyāna?”
At Ge’u Lake, [Zhaozhou] held up his whisk and made a dot in the air. The Dharma Master was at a loss.
Emperor Xianzong said, "The Dharma Master has lectured on infinite sutras and śāstras, yet he cannot cope with this single dot. The Master replied, "To apply a circle to fit a square."
Holding a square to fit a circle—once gained, once lost; the Heavenly Mirror is clearly manifest.
At the request of the assembly at Sike Yuanjue Monastery for a small discourse, this old, decrepit fellow acts with feigned innocence, winning nothing but a daily pittance of a few sheng and he.
Along the official highway, he idly pushes his cart crosswise; in many places, he attempts to force a square peg into a round hole. Sometimes, when encountering the noble, he treats them as common.
Passing through Sīkṣī Town and crossing Shílín Pass—at a place where the waters flow so tightly they cannot be diverted—the eastern gate opens wide.

When one has withdrawn oneself to yield to others, yet strikes and plunders right within the nest. After achieving great penetration and seizing the opportune moment, the rites and music of the Three Dynasties still remain.
Here, the guest listens while the host decides: how shall you meet the assembly? (He strikes the whisk and says: A swift opportunity is difficult to encounter.
Again, it is recounted: When Linji visited Longguang, he said, "Without deploying a sharp point of wit, how can one achieve victory? Longguang sat firmly in his seat.
Linji said, "Great Master of Good Knowledge, do you have no skillful means? Longguang stared at him with wide eyes and said, "Ha! Linji clapped his hands and said:
"This old fellow has met with defeat today. The Master said: "Seated in solemn repose beneath the oil-silk banner, from where could a formidable foe have come?
The signal drums were clearly heard; they withdrew while still holding their banners. Do you all see these two elders?
This Dharma talk is shown to the Chan practitioner Sào:
From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past, not a single dharma has been given to anyone; it is only valued that each person retreats to themselves and presses on until they reach [the realization].
There is no place for the application of the mind; it is encountered spontaneously, as if by chance. It is like a furious lion tearing at stone, or a venomous dragon churning the sea.

Only then does one know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have not bestowed a single dharma upon anyone. Often, these days, my fellow practitioners do not suffer from a lack of intelligence in their capacity.
Yet they suffer from being unable to blunt their own cleverness; fearing that others will say they do not understand, they simply cling to the present light and its objects.
Their frantic machinations and evil perceptions are like dung beetles clutching their dung-balls, considering themselves to have attained realization, unaware of what true attainment actually is.

It is not like that. If one is a true member of the lineage of the Way, possessing the spirit and resolve that refuses to submit even to Buddhas and patriarchs, let alone the tracks and byways of the present age—even empty space must be overturned. Moving freely in every direction, they carry forth the Great Function.
Only then can one be considered a peerless herb among the multitude; thus, you shall not bring shame upon yourself. Chan practitioner Miao possesses a keen and sharp nature.

Having reached this point in your practice and having been at Ciyun for three years, the autumn wind has stirred your aspirations, and you have shaken the staff of your travels to seek further exhortation.
This old fool has nothing more to say. Written on the day before the ninth of the ninth month in the Baoyu era.

To show the junior monk Qingzheng the phrase that provides power for a wandering journey: grasp its essence before there were Buddhas or Patriarchs; otherwise, you have already fallen into the secondary.
If you leave one monastery and enter another community, you will become entangled in the vines of ten thousand households; how could you ever find clarity? You must know the primary cause.
A man of sharp intelligence is like a *kalaviṅka* chick that has already shed its shell and outgrown its ordinary feathers;

even if he has not yet attained a single blow of the "understanding-ground," his firm and resolute resolve is naturally different from others. Xuefeng went to Touzi three times and ascended to Dongshan nine times.
Taking a hand-towel and hanging it around his neck, he served as the cook wherever he went, performing manual labor without weariness.
When he first met Deshan, he asked about matters concerning the Dharma-gate: "Does a student have any share in this? Deshan struck him with his staff upon hearing the question and further told him:
"In my school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma to give to others. Langdang...
"Little. At that moment, Xuefeng was like one whose bucket-bottom has fallen away. Yet, what can be done about the matters of the School of the Lineage?

He went all the way to Aoshan, where during a snowy night he confessed every detail to Yantou. Suddenly, [Yantou] let out a thunderous roar and said, "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure.
Instantly, everything upon which he had previously placed his reliance vanished from sight. In a flurry, he cried out: "Now..."
Today is the day the Tortoise Mountain attained the Way; yet who was it that caused this to happen? When I, Chingzheng, previously left Sichuan, the monk was here;
this must surely be due to a karmic affinity from former lives. Once the single mat is spread and the wooden board is struck, one may appear quite outstanding.

However, compared to earlier times, both the pursuit of the ultimate essence (*zongqu*) and the analysis of the lineage of words (*yumo*) are ailments. In my observations of those nowadays who pursue the ultimate essence:
Most people engage in deliberations on the "real Dharma. Those who understand the capacity of others follow in their footsteps;
since you neither deliberate on the real Dharma nor permit following in others' footsteps, how should I reach a decisive judgment? Wait until you have returned from your travels of universal study.
There is another point for examination:
if one shows diligent practitioners the way of herding and leads them toward indolence, they will not know who is the person and who is the ox. Looking back at the past, [it is clear].
To enter the grass and drag [the ox] back is merely to twist and wring it in vain; even a foot-rule and a whip, or an inch of rope, become superfluous things.
Since you have already reached this point, if you turn toward that other side to practice, then for those who encounter the matter of "dropping the hand," all shall have their noses pierced.
You must truly reach this stage before you can succeed. The Chan practitioner Qin from Jiangyou is one who studies the art of herding.
I once counted among the ranks of a single cell at Ciyun Monastery. Now, having come from Yujia to take my leave, you have presented me with the words bestowed upon you by various elders;
therein I learned that you were known as "Lazy Herder" (Lanmu). I therefore said to him: "A herder is one who herds himself. If he does not herd, he is finished.
Only when herding reaches the point of laziness is there a field for rest. This is what the monastic community expects of you."
It is so. Nevertheless, I still have a question. In the past, Master Lan was lazy regarding other matters but diligent in tending his flock;

thus it is said: "The path stretches far and wide; how pitiable! Even if you try to chase him away, he will not go. This is to tend the flock for the rest of one's life without ever having to tend it.
If one were diligent regarding other matters but lazy in tending the flock, then one would tread upon the neighbor's field. Furthermore, if one were lazy regarding other matters...
Idle in herding? For now, do not speak of dreams; simply look directly here, observing with true scrutiny.
Suddenly, when neither person nor ox is seen, you will return home and sit in peace; this truly constitutes being idle in herding.
The Verse-Old Case cites Chan Master Baizhang Weizheng, who addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, help me clear the fields;
I shall preach the Great Meaning for you. A monk said, "The fields have been cleared; we pray that the Master will preach the Great Meaning. Baizhang walked several paces.
He spreads his two hands.

Mazu then raised the case of Magu asking a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk stepped forward and said, "I am not well. Magu asked again; the monk withdrew.

The monk said, "It is very much like being sightless. Gu let go of him and said, "I release your life and allow you to breathe."

The monk prostrated himself. Gu again seized him by the collar; the monk pulled back his arm and departed. Gu said, "Do not take a three-year-old bamboo and attempt to compare it with a ten-thousand-year-old pine."

From this point on, the military arts prize the subduing of schemes; capturing the enemy through fierce combat is not considered supreme. Deeply resonant are the *diaodou* drums under the moon of the third watch;
the majesty of the jade command tent extends through the autumn of the Purple Barrier.
Citing the public case of Aṅgulimāla rescuing a woman in childbirth:
Suddenly one sees the dragon boat surging over the waves; The drum beats with urgency, the flute sounds mournful. When the silken prize reaches his hands, he lets it go lightly;
But when he turns his head back, the matter has already changed.
Linji went back to his home region during the summer retreat to visit his parents. Upon meeting Huangbo while the latter was reading a sutra, Linji said, "I thought you were someone special;
it turns out you are just an old monk who soaks black beans. After staying for several days, he took his leave. Huangbo said:
"You have broken the summer retreat; why not stay until it is finished? Linji said, "I have come for a moment to pay my respects to the Master.
Baizhang struck him and ordered him to leave. On the way back, Linji harbored doubts about this matter and returned to complete the summer retreat.
In my old garden, the red and purple flowers bloom of their own accord; they do not wait for the spring breeze to blow with intent.
By the time the traveler turns his head back once more, the fragrant snow upon the branches has already fallen in profusion.
I cite the ancient worthy’s kōan of eating oil-cakes at the shrine.
As soon as he was greedy for them, he was caught by them; in that interval, half-revealed yet entirely concealed. Who now is the bystander?
A single laugh—why trouble to hang it upon one's teeth?
Dazu [Zhaozhou] cites an instance where Guishan addressed the assembly, saying: "The bitter cold of mid-winter is an annual occurrence; as the movement of the sun's shadow shifts, what is the matter?
Yangshan crossed his hands, stepped forward, and stood there. Guishan said, "I knew well that you could not answer this question.
He then looked toward Xiangyan and asked, "And how about you? Xiangyan said, "I can certainly answer this."
[Mañjuśrī] spoke. Guishan [Miaoxian] brought up the previous conversation. Yanguan also joined his palms and stepped forward to stand. Guishan said, "Fortunately, Jizi (Mañjuśrī) does not understand;
he blows a flute with no holes and accompanies it by clapping felt and wooden boards. Father and son are in harmony, yet ice and charcoal are opposites—this is the pivot of the final moment."
As for the result: originally, Dingzhou produced fine porcelain bowls.
Juegeng Qing asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "From Sanfeng. Qing said, "Where did you spend the summer?
The monk said, "At Wufeng. Qing said, "I grant you thirty blows. The monk said, "Where was my fault? Qing—
It is said: For your sake, I leave one grove to enter another.
With a single beat of the drum, a fragrant breeze arrives from the south; once more proceeding, a jade moon hangs upon the azure pines.
While the young gentlemen at the brocade banquet are still deeply intoxicated, the white snow and the secluded orchids remain in vain, though repeated three times.
A monk asked Luopu, "Do you still receive those who can overturn heaven and earth? Luopu held up his whisk.
The monk said, "In that case, one has met a wise sovereign. Luopu said, "It is like a melody that is barely worth listening to, yet is blown by the wind into another tune."
"Alas! A single fox-spirit from an ancient tomb, having transformed into a human, sought to deceive others. Before the ornamental pillar was even erected, it was already ruined;
until now, there has been no place for it to hide its body."
Xuefeng once, while on a communal work assignment, was carrying a bundle of rattan vines himself. On the road, he encountered a monk; he immediately threw the bundle down.
As the monk reached out to pick it up, Xuefeng gave him a kick. Upon returning, Xuefeng recounted this to Changsheng, saying, "Today I kicked that monk thoroughly.
Changsheng said, "Only when you, Master, take the place of that monk and enter the Nirvana Hall will you have truly finished. Thereupon, Xuefeng stopped speaking.

Go; let us cease discussing the phoenix-feathered arrow shot at the bird’s nest. Behold the empty bow that brings down the nine-tufted eagle. How could its release and withdrawal escape the hand of Houyi?
To assist by drawing the string beside him is likewise in vain.
Citing Zhaozhou’s question to Touzi: “When a person who has undergone the great death returns to life, what is it like? Touzi said:
“Night travel is not permitted; one must arrive by dawn.”
Two ears do not fit together nor can they share a shoulder; as soon as a poisonous hand is extended, an old fist shall strike in return.
Today we ascend to heaven with the azure void; tomorrow we enter the earth with the Yellow Springs.
A monk asked Dongshan, "When cold and heat arrive, how can one avoid them? Dongshan said, "Why not go to a place where there is neither cold nor heat?
The monk asked, "What is this place where there is neither cold nor heat? Dongshan said, "When it is cold, the cold kills you;
when it is hot, the heat kills you."

The traveler drifts upon the divine raft, trespassing through the Ox and Plow constellations; the Milky Way and the azure seas flow on in secret communion. Mount Kunlun is toppled, leaving nothing to rely upon;
ten thousand miles of vast sky share the same autumnal hue.
Yantou asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "From the Western Capital.
Yantou said, "After Huang Chao passed through, did you manage to recover your sword? The monk said, "I recovered it. Yantou extended his neck and said, "Kill!
The monk said, "The Master’s head has fallen! Yantou laughed loudly. Later, the monk went to Xuefeng, and Xuefeng asked, "Where have you come from? The monk said—
Yantou arrived. Feng asked, "What words did he say? The monk recounted the previous conversation. Feng struck him twenty blows and drove him out.
When one displays valor and raises the banner, there is no great adversary; yet look, the body is already trapped within a heavy siege. One must seize the horns and charge through the pass.
"Go. He mounted his carriage with a green dragon, yet did not dismount from his horse.
Once, when a monk came to take leave of Master Yangshan, Yangshan made a stroke with his hand; the monk did not depart.
Yangshan made another stroke, and the monk left. Master Dayu Zhi said: "Why did he not [depart] after the first stroke?"
It goes away. After one stroke, why does it then go away? Do you understand? The first stroke and the last stroke together form two strokes.
A hungry man greedily craves food, yet the good farmer’s grain; a thirsty man mistakenly drinks the water of a house infested with venomous insects. Face-to-face, they become a thousand miles apart.
"Yao! A bandit possesses a wisdom that surpasses that of a gentleman. He says:
'When I do not see, why do you not see the place where I do not see? If you were to see my non-seeing, it would naturally not be the characteristic of that non-seeing.

What is it that you lack?
By Zhang Gong’s house, mulberry and hemp reach the very edge; in Li Lao’s garden, nothing but flowers are grown. The scenery before one’s eyes is infinitely beautiful;
laughing, he calls out to pour from the silver bowl the flowing rosy clouds.
Qianfeng raised his staff and addressed the assembly, saying, "The Dharma-body has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance;

you must penetrate each one thoroughly before you can sit securely. At that time, Yunmen stepped forward from the assembly and asked, "Why does the person inside the hermitage not see what is outside the hermitage?
Qianfeng laughed heartily. Yunmen said, "This is still a point of doubt for a student. Qianfeng [nodded].
Xuefeng said, "What kind of mental activity is this, my son? Muzhou said, "I also want the Master to understand thoroughly. Xuefeng said, "Only then can you sit securely.
The river surface is windless and as level as a mirror; yet upon turning one's head, shifting moods present themselves anew. Fengyi rides the waves—how perilous and difficult!"
Shè. A fisherman was rowing his boat with a skill as marvelous as that of a god.
He pointed to the King of Kasmira, who was holding a sword and asked the twenty-fourth patriarch, Master Shizi, saying, "Have you attained the emptiness of the aggregates?
The patriarch replied, "I have attained the emptiness of the aggregates. The king said, "Have you transcended birth and death? The patriarch replied, "I have transcended them."
"Life and death. The King said, "Since you have transcended life and death, you may give me your head. The Patriarch replied, "This body is not mine; how much less so this head?
The King then struck off his head, whereupon white milk surged forth several *zhang* high, and the King's own arm fell away.
Xuefeng said, "How great was Master Shizi, yet even his head could not act as its own master! Xuedou said, "A true adept!"
O King, nature’s course is fixed:
leaves fall as the wind rises and autumn comes to heaven and earth. The long river rolls on, flowing only toward the east. The traveler does not pluck the willows by the parting pavilion;
the Qiang flute plays empty notes of sorrow at the setting sun.
The Senior Monk Huinuo went to Baizhang. Baizhang said, "I have a question I wish to ask you; would that be permissible?
Huinuo said, "Fortunately, it is not a matter of words; why must you prattle on? Baizhang said, "If that is so, then I grant you leave to ask. Huinuo said, "Please, give me another cup of tea.
Baizhang said, "Having secured Annam, you are now anxious about the north of the pass. Huinuo split open his chest and said, "It is like this."
"It is so," [Zhao]zhou said. "Nevertheless, it is difficult to grasp; nevertheless, it is difficult to grasp. Huineng said, "If you know it, you have attained it.

As for skillful warfare, how does it compare to skillful strategy? The military arts of Sun Wu and Wu Qi—how could they be their peers? Observe the formations at the ancient frontier passes in the autumn wind."
The Power: The same surroundings, yet two kinds of sorrow.
A Verse in Praise of the Buddha by the Patriarchs (with appended verse).
The Image of Leaving the Mountains.
Entering the mountains, he possessed the auspicious markings of a dragon and the noble quality of a phoenix; emerging from the mountains, he appeared in tattered robes and disheveled appearance.
To further analyze what he has awakened to is merely to add another layer of muddied confusion.

The Great Being of Potalaka dwells where heaven and sea merge in profound stillness; the coastal cliffs stand solitary and remote. To perceive this with intimacy is like driving a wedge into empty space, as the raging surges pound the moon before the crags to pieces.

The beauty of the horse-herder’s wife casts glances as alluring as the moon; she constantly upholds the sixty thousand words [of the Lotus Sūtra]. Upon the sands of Jinshe, amidst the waves of the five desires, the moon rises.
This is the response of the Great Being (Bodhisattva) to King Yue.
The mountains of the sea are jagged and precipitous; the ocean waves crash and pound; the sea winds sweep and caress; the sea clouds drift and soar.

When one looks up at the Sun of Wisdom that shatters the darkness, who could fail to perceive its illumination? Beholding the Gate of Universal Radiance (Samantamukha) that requires no lock, one departs for the directionless realm.

Where response and stimulus meet in mutual resonance, it is unfathomable and immeasurable. One from beyond the borders offers sincere devotion, and the shadow of Bodhi appears. I speak thus, increasing the gold.
He used yellow [clothing].
When crossing water in a cloth bag, if it was deep he waded;
if shallow, he lifted it up. At the seventy-two shallows, no wind or waves arose.
The Cloth Bag Tuṣita Heaven; the jurisdiction of Changting. The cloth bag is flung open; buying for oneself and selling for oneself.
Blinking one's eyebrows—lost, lost!
Vimalakīrti’s room is a mere enclosure; his ground is but ten *hù* square. Alas, Vimalakīrti! His illness lies right here.
Fenggan, Hanzhi, and Shishi— [all fall within this same trap.]
From where do you come? Where do you go? What do you expect of these two sons? With a tiger’s gaze, he stares intently;
amidst the dark, chilling winds, the cold mountain is swept—swept by the horizontal, swept by the vertical. Even the Teacher of the Seven Buddhas is left in no small measure of disarray.

Shide’s act of collecting vegetable scraps was a single stroke that left no room for further maneuver; it cut off all manifold distinctions. His "wondrous answer" poured from a jar, sticking to his teeth and gums.
How could this compare to stealing the Buddha’s rice and vegetable scraps while inside Guoqing Temple?
When Dharma crossed over the reeds, Nan-tou questioned him;
he did not answer well and departed toward the north. They were not in accord. He claimed to have "trod upon" [the truth], yet there was no connection at all.
Where there are no branches or leaves, branches and leaves spread out in every direction; where there is no wind or wave, wind and waves swirl all around.

The single flower of Bodhidharma was transplanted from the West; its five petals now emit a brilliant fragrance. Those who smell the stamens and seek the blossoms swarm about like bees and butterflies.
The earth is vast and the heavens are wide; it is difficult to map the spreading of these tendrils.
The Arhat’s lotus-stalk hollow conceals his body without leaving even a single trace; he stirs up wind and clouds, and his bounty pervades the great earth.
Whether hidden or manifest, whether great or small, these differences can ultimately never escape the vessel of his capacity. Before those with clear eyes, such things are not to be disparaged.
How admirable! Alas!
The "Diagram of the Mutual Courtesy between the Two Chan Masters Dàhuì and Hóngzhì" depicts their countenances both grave and smiling;
a profusion of harmonious spirit flows from them. One precedes and the other follows, transcending all and leaving the dust behind. Their faces, once marred by miasma, suddenly become radiant.

Ah! A swift thunderclap is about to burst forth. Horned skulls sprout like frost; withered wood gives birth to spring. To face the enemy from both front and rear is to pay a hundred thousand for a neighbor.
It is easy to get along when meeting others, but difficult to act as one when sharing a common task.
The destiny of Heaven is vast and far-reaching;
the era of the Diwu (Eastern Jin) dynasty has come to its end. People vie with one another to seek their place of refuge on Mount Lu. What is the purpose of dredging ponds and planting lotus roots?
How many times have I gazed upon the hanging drum from the Western Hills? Yuanming, who loved wine, could not be persuaded to stay; Lingyun, who craved the Buddha, pushed him away.
I shall not go. Let us set aside for now the two or three points of our alliance. Alas! Where are you now?

When Master Yuan and Lu Xiujing meet with a single smile, all lingering resentment naturally dissolves. To erect barriers is to turn one's own liver and gall into Chu and Yue; to transcend the physical form is to—
The great Peng and the small gull enjoy their carefree wanderings; with a refreshing spirit so pure and bright, what need is there for the breeze from the Crane Chariot?
With sleeves gracefully raised in parting, one does not see the Tiger Brook Bridge. This is one of the six matters of Donglin, and its noble character can still be envisioned.
The ancients cannot be brought back, and the present cannot be summoned. Fire gives birth to lotus flowers; snow grows banana trees.
Our late teacher, National Teacher Beijian (invited by Master Renlao Jiaozhong):
"Pah! Pah! Pah! Who is this person? Barefoot, he circles all around Mount Sumeru. Lacking any skillful means, he watches as a guest comes to see a thief and waits for the thief to strike.
Furthermore, he awaits the moment when the thief’s eyes flicker. Homage, homage! Master Jiaozhong was once poisoned by him."
I do not yet know how to repay the service of the campaign at the East Gate.
Master Dongshan Yuan (invited by Qiaowu):
Inside the gate are insects and inside the chamber is poison; as soon as one passes the Lingxiao Peak, the entire family falls into discord, pointing to white as black.
Ah! This substance provides proof for the grievance of having a head. Shifting the mode and altering the melody, it sings forth a tune beyond any score.
From Fusha in Fengchuan to the deep recesses of Jianchi—who has walked this path with me?

There is no need for the heights of Xiangguyi Rock; one must know that what has been unfurled shall not be retracted. When the nine-fold phoenix arrives, the woodcutter’s song is sufficient for a single Kui. This is the private inheritance.
Do not conceal it. Leave it entirely sealed, even in its half-folds. Whether you praise it or revile it, your mouth will go mute and your tongue will fall out.

The Dharma Master Wankong has grown horns upon his eyes; he carries a needle in his bag and drives along ancient ruts, opening a level road that reaches the Dragon Canon while forgetting the fish-trap.
Ah! He reveals the vast expanse of the sky of righteousness. Grasping the fly-whisk upside down, he overturns the surging waves of eloquent debate.
With a majestic array and a straight-forward banner, he takes as wrong what others deem right, and as right what others deem wrong; he unfurls the strategic maneuvers of the "Long啸" (Lao-xiao).
A scion of the lineage of Master Moulho; after his *nirvāṇa*, who could have known that he would borrow the tongues of the myriad phenomena?
— By the Buddhist monk Sungsong.

He upheld the essential tenets of the school that possesses the perfect fusion of all virtues, and magnified his family’s reputation by transmitting the lineage of the "Attainmentless Transmission of the Way.
He cultivated the four samādhis with solemnity while personally practicing with single-minded diligence; he analyzed the four dharma-realms, thereby delighting the imperial heart of the Nine Palaces.
Sweeping away the hives of bees and the mounds of ants, he established himself as a master of the Great Dharma, a monk like a phoenix.
Master Yihǔ was a paragon for upholding the school; his writings were as brilliant as the constellation Ki-pi, causing the Prajñā to shine ever more brightly.
His robes were of golden brocade, causing the Way of the Dharma to flourish ever more gloriously. As for the succession of the lineage from Nāgārjuna, the Imperial Mind propagated it separately.

When it was time to speak, he remained in profound silence; when it was time to remain silent, he was luminously clear. This is what is meant by the confluence of a hundred rivers, all flowing toward the Great Ocean.
Master Huī of Hangu explored the ancestral temple with vigor;
Yitian cut across horizontally, and Nanhū’s rain of flowers repeatedly took the foremost rank. The Three Contemplations stand like three peaks amidst the misty tigers and leopards;
the One Vehicle is distinguished as the tailgate that naturally drains away. The sea is vast and the mountains remote; it is difficult to follow in their tracks.
Regarding the tracks [of his legacy]: who can seek the spring in the cold valley when the clouds are warm? On clear nights, the moon again shines brightly across the vast sky.

Dharma Master Zhangyun was stalwart and imposing, compassionate, harmonious, and serene; his reputation resounded throughout the rivers and lakes. As for his character, his appearance, and his standing within the Tiantai school, he was truly eminent.
In the enumeration of Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle, the "one" and the "three" do not stand as separate entities. The *Sūtra* is like a finger pointing at the moon;

once the finger and the moon are both forgotten, one is awakened in all four directions and the four flowers fly upward. Before aging, one conceals the light and returns to the Constantly Quiescent Light (*sada-prabhāsvara*).
This is precisely why he was the one who upheld the lineage of the Baotang school—the master Yungong Hanzhang.
Elder Yungu Cui (requested by his junior disciple):

As empty as clouds, as vast as a valley, he dwells in a single hermitage at year’s end amidst a thousand clusters of lakes and mountains. Teacher and disciple have forgotten each other—why need one strike the back like Guling?
There is no interval between movement and stillness—why did Taling needlessly kick his feet in frustration? With a single flavor, roll up the tongue and settle the mind in silent contemplation.
Entrusting the transmission of the *Songfeng* melodies. When the Jade Table is thus modulated, it is like calling "five" instead of "six.
Zen Master Zhiyan’s harmonious aura is as lush as a cluster of mushrooms; yet when touched, they turn into thorns. He laughs as he takes a confident step that overturns Mount Lingxiao. Directly!

He attained the realization of the New Chang Stone Buddha, from whose brow perspiration issued. At the summit of Mount Ciyun, his spiritual function was unhindered in all directions; he soared through the air and traversed the void, establishing himself according to his will.
The towering peaks of Gaolun are azure and vast, and the Eastern Lake is shrouded in mist. Even the marvelous brushwork of the monk Zhaoyou would find it difficult to transmit its likeness.
Not moving a single hair, yet leaving everything in disarray.

*Ei!* As for the Lecturer, his mouth gapes and his brows are knit; he sits like a driven stake. The fragrance of his precepts blows against the wind; he travels alone, braving the frost. He has newly received the scriptures.

He esteemed the fundamental source. As the three presiding masters maintained the mainstays of the Dharma community, this was how he brought forth the Vinaya-piṭaka from the tip of a single hair and erected the banner of diligence for the final age.

Dharma Master Guo of Nanjian possessed a serene temperament and a dignified countenance; his breadth of character was as vast as the sky. He was like lingering snow upon a spring ridge, or the moon at its zenith over an autumn river.

Standing tall amidst the clouds, his golden and azure robes enhanced the wondrous view of the "Small Flying Peak"; he brought forth the hidden depths of former sages, arriving during the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty.
The lingering fragrance of his legacy is seen and heard by some; thus, their delusions dissolve and their minds are subdued. As for his own life, he was simple and austere;
in his dealings with others, he was compassionate and dignified. He did not cling to the literal letter of the texts, nor did he fall into mundane indifference.
This is how he became the true heir to Beifeng, and within the samādhi of self-enjoyment, he harmonized with the fundamental principles of the school of inherent nature.

Dharma Master Yimeng’s countenance was emaciated yet his demeanor was exalted. In the ancient waters of Qian and the clear streams of the Xiao, he was as beautiful as a pearl reflecting the light of the moon.

Having forgotten the fishing trap of the Mahāyāna sūtras, not a single drop adhered to names and characteristics; having darkly attained the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), not a single hair clung to the profound mysteries. At Stone Gorge—

Entrusting the robe: the final current is the oracle. Amidst mountain thunder and mountain springs, one follows the teachings to form a name; when the void itself understands the lecture, who is there to know it?
The Layman Shanyin (appearing with a shaven head and square monk’s robe) was a monk in form and a paragon among men.
What did he do? He always wore his field-weed robes. What did he speak? He constantly brandished his jade fly-whisk.
His worldly sentiments were as vast and leisurely as autumn clouds, light and thin; the clarity within his breast was like the hanging autumn moon.
His brilliance is luminous; his endowment is numinous; his bestowal is impartial. The six apertures are naturally vacant, and the myriad phenomena naturally manifest.
Who is this person? Is he not one who does not enter the mountain forests to hide, yet does not need to bathe in the Canglang River to become pure?
Fan Luwei requested a eulogy for his mother, Lady Chen, on her part as a model of maternal virtue.

Her kindness and gentleness were the standard for the inner quarters; she maintained the domestic code with steadfastness. Her virtuous deeds were as pure as ice and snow; her longevity was like the pine and cypress.

Upon the hall, she was composed and graceful, like a phoenix amidst the clouds; beneath the hall, her children were gathered in great numbers, like orchids and jade. Her profound virtue was stored in secret, leaving behind...

Through successive generations, harmonious breath and concord have permeated the neighboring villages. Matching the masters of the eastern city, they entrust the Buddha-body to the illusion of equality;
wielding the swift faculty of Candraprabha, they remain ever-intimate with daily life.
If one asks where the turning point lies within this, it is as if one were to measure out empty space—wondrous and without a trace.
To praise oneself is to involve oneself in this realm; to encounter conditions is not to borrow from them. To follow along with the wicked is to be surpassed by those who delight in them.

To cast aside the surplus words of the thousand sages as mere painted mountains and rivers, and to laugh at the triggering of the mechanism by those of old as being like tying knots in a headcloth to catch rabbits or horses—this allows not even a single thread of impurity to enter.
Pause. The handle of the void arises. Right now, having met with defeat, toward whom do you direct it? It is better to revile yourself than to revile others.
Elder Baofu Pu requested a eulogy for Yunmen’s "Universal" (Pǔ). A crossbow of a thousand *jīn*:
released all at once, the arrow passes through the shield when facing the target. When there is a head to the grievance, there is a creditor to the debt.
Master.
Elder Faxi Jing requests a verse of praise:
Without a fixed standard and beyond conceptual grasp, opening one’s mouth leads to erroneous deliberation. Iron caltrops are solid and firm; the sun is cold and the moon is hot.
The Jing River is clear and the Wei River is turbid. Last night, a phoenix nested and gave birth to a young phoenix (yuezhu).
Elder Jifu Jian requests a eulogy:
thundering like lightning, every inch and fraction of a hair is the total function of the Great Utility. Setting down the bamboo cane, Yunmen emerges.
Gùjiàn yī! Elder Mínghuà requests a eulogy:
acting without acting, benefiting without benefiting, his harmonious spirit is like spring; one cannot draw near to him, yet at times he appears in perilous places.
With little artifice, he overthrows Linji, that thief who steals in broad daylight. Retaliation for an injury with an injury—the principle is unerring.
For the request of Elder Yi to provide a eulogy:
[毯-炎+畏][毯-炎+畏][毯-炎+崔][毯-炎+崔]. Lofty and towering, he forces his way to the forefront; indeed, one sees his eccentricity, as straight as split bamboo.
Yet few people know its curves and circles; it is like rolling a ball along, yet I always employ its straight edges.

Hearing that my school is most extraordinary, you should consider it for many years as nothing more than a broom-handle or a tree stump. To build a plank road openly while crossing Chen-cang in secret—when words are uttered, there are no inscriptions upon monuments;
when examining a thief, one does not require physical evidence. How dare you recklessly claim to be the direct descendants of the Huapu-gua?
Truly, it is as the saying goes: "The rice is gone, leaving only the husk. Such a mouth is so closed that not only do others loathe it, but I loathe it myself.
How could it bear to be rendered in ink and color and hung in a high hall? First, entrust this severed cloud to the element of fire for safekeeping;
once water has been spilled, it cannot be recovered. Let the four seas boil like boiling broth—it matters not.
Elder Yong of West Mountain requested a eulogy for the tethered empty clouds and stems.
To mend the vast void, one must indeed rely on others to bring forth its function, even when situated within the hands of the destitute.
Casually bumping into an old enemy; lively and unrestrained, he is seized and handled on the spot.
Elder Qizhen invited me to praise his "no-self.
Yet this fellow—before one can even blink an eye, the talk has already fallen into error. He turns over his skin, refusing to let others pass.
He smashed the "Jade of Ten Thousand Cities" and unleashed the calamity upon the people of Qin.
Līzhōu Jiè, the Elder, requested that we assist one another in praising him;
yet he himself picked up and toyed with it, deceiving those who rely on others and causing the destruction of the Hu race. The karma lies within this very act.
He was unaware of it himself. When Jiu Cheng gathered the *Shao* music at Mount Dan, the phoenixes of the mountain assembled.
His junior disciple Qingmo requested a eulogy for him:
"Straight as a hook, curved as a string; he sends the blind along, with none able to fathom how it is so. Unable to understand his deep crouching, I have forced myself to emerge."
Before others, he remains silent, yet his intent is transmitted; one must wait for a donkey’s year [for it to be fully realized].
Disciple Qingtai requested a eulogy:
"A flash of joy, a flash of anger; headless and brainless. When the Way prevails and the times are peaceful, wind arises from a mere stir. A casual collision."
A black-lacquered bamboo whisk comes slashing across the face; there is no Zen to discuss. With a three-inch tongue, one sweeps through chaos;
from the nines and nines to the hundreds and hundreds, one remains unaware of growing old. To call oneself a descendant of Linji—what a stubborn stone has ever been a treasure!
The junior monk Qing Rui requested a eulogy for the *weiwuirui* (a type of medicinal herb).
[He] repeatedly knotted it, yet could not hold it steady; many people were displeased. He followed the void with a single flavor, emptying the void itself.
Who knows what he might have said? It is like the "Instruction on Finding the Lost Child" for raising a child—amidst the scorching heat of the sixth month, a miraculous omen drifts down.
Snow. A Verse in Praise of Chancellor Qiuhue, the State Preceptor.
I prostrate to the Dharmakāya Lord Vairocana, the Perfectly Awakened One in whom the three bodies are one essence; to Mañjuśrī, the great ocean of wisdom;
to Samantabhadra, the gateway of pure conduct and vows; to the Great Compassionate Father Avalokiteśvara;

and to the fifty-three spiritual friends of the stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, and the bhūmis, as well as the celestial dragons and spirits who protect through both provisional and ultimate means—may their compassionate majesty descend upon us.

Majestic above, he gazes upon this offering of praise as his daily practice fills the void. On the eighth day of the second month of autumn in the year Guiyou, a wondrous person was born in the Golden Land of Dīpaṃkara.

From before the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranirghoṣa Tathāgata, he has upheld the primary cause; on Mount Lingyan, he received the prediction of enlightenment. A *utpala* flower conceives its marvel and appears but once in an age;
the constellation Mao sends forth its essence as an auspicious sign between heaven and earth. It is at such a time that the assembly of a thousand spirits gathers in celebration.

The way of sovereign and minister harmonized like the joining of tally-sticks; the scale of the ascendant peace was ever more steadfast and grave. With a breath he transformed emergencies and constantly stabilized the floating world.
He sacrificed his person for the state’s perils, entering deep into danger; with his own hands he supported the sun’s chariot-wheel as it ascended to the midst of heaven.

Distant barbarians shrank back in awe of his majesty and strategy; the common people flourished in joy, resting secure upon their mats. The succeeding Emperor took him as a model and honored him as a teacher; all myriad creatures—
We look up to you and rely on you as our very life. As the Buddha-dharma spreads, it illuminates a flourishing age; those who uphold the world and protect the Dharma truly have a firm foundation.
Viewing today from two thousand years hence, it will be no different than it was two thousand years ago. May the life-force of the Tathāgata’s wisdom continue forever.
May the right faith of sentient beings never be severed; may there be the great power to rectify heaven and earth, and the great merit to bring peace and happiness to the common people.

Here in this monastery on the eastern side of Mount Mao, presided over by the relics of Śākyamuni Buddha, stands this auspicious and most excellent site where a long-life shrine has been established for the majestic and radiant image of the Buddha.
Now, a vast multitude of monastics have solemnly gathered, with the sounding of bells and drums and the chanting of *brahman* hymns.
What is there to be wished for? All phenomena and all beings upon their tongues proclaim long life. The precious stūpa manifests, radiating auspicious light.
In the past, King Aśoka constructed Buddha-stūpas, numbering eighty-four thousand in total. Within each single stūpa were eighty-four thousand; within those eighty-four thousand was a single stūpa.
Within that single stūpa were eighty-four thousand Mañjuśrīs and eighty-four thousand most excellent ones. May [all be fulfilled].
May all be auspicious and sublime; may they scatter the boundless springtime of the realm of longevity.
Inscribed at the Two Pools of the "Hall for Transforming Objects" of the Layman Juexin.
Two pools glisten with cold, azure waters; a single hall embraces vast tranquility. Tall willows meet the spring as fresh emerald hues unfold; cold plum blossoms brighten in the clearing sky.
The snow is pure and the fragrance is profuse; well-tended in its original state, it remains ever in full bloom. One observes the exchange of fragrances through the four seasons;
the realm of miscellaneous flowers pervades every atom within the lands. The ten *pāramitās* further act as both primary and secondary elements.

The awakened mind rests upon the armrest, wandering at ease; the six faculties are all wondrous, with nothing to subdue. Seated in *padmāsana*, neither speaking nor remaining silent, a single curl of incense smoke lingers as the spring day draws long.
What did Old Śākyamuni see? His three hundred discourses were all skillful means. Among them, one point is most intimate: to transform things rather than being transformed by things.
In this hall, every single thing is fundamentally no different; it is only according to how people utilize them that there is intimacy or distance.
Every mote of dust is subsumed within the Great Vairocana. One should laugh [at the notion] that originally, things neither undergo transformation nor cease to exist.
The person takes my burden and I take their share; they deceive me in myriad ways. A single string of golden locks—how cold the bones!
What a fine merchant never stops peddling dead goods, clearly carrying them out for all to see.
Showing the True Travel of the Venerable Scholar Zhao Jinping:
Who cares that the traveler’s journey is far? How many times has the spring breeze passed over the flowers in the Kunlun Garden?
If you understand that worlds are hidden within a grain of millet, then Liaoyang is not merely the Jade Imperial Palace.
The nature of emptiness encompasses all phenomena, equaling the vast void. Yet one must still set aside Zhaozhou’s “no. If you wish now to know the ultimate point:
Śūnyatā has newly grown a beard beneath his chin.

Transcending all verbal expression, as he expounds upon the void, the four flowers fly; the great earth, mountains, and rivers all respond with a single impulse. Though one searches among the blue-eyed and yellow-headed, there is nowhere to find him;
herein, from the very beginning, he has never moved his lips.
The Japanese attendant returns home;
within the three responses, the secret meaning is communicated. Clearly, rice and cloth wrap the spring breeze. Cease arguing over intimacy or lack thereof;
the great ship returns its course to the East Sea.
The Way is once again the trunk;
he receives guests and establishes a dwelling nestled among the clouds and mountains. The atmosphere of the ancient spring has returned. To anyone who passes through the gate, he bids them rest;
who would say that the Way-teacher lacks ingenuity?
The soothsayer Wang Zhenzhai says:
"When the mouth speaks of Heaven, there is Zhenzhai. The five elements never involve deliberate arrangement. Sitting opposite in the small studio, it seems as though there is no speech;
how many times have bright clouds passed over the broken cliffs?"
Hé Dàyuán has left Zifu to dwell at Bāiyún;
he has cast down his ladle for scooping the stream and shifted his axe to the mountains in the deep recesses. Tell this to the guests outside the gates of Bāiyún:
when you meet him, do not look upon him as you did before.
While ill, I saw off Attendant Zhan for the capital, parting leisurely by the side of my medicinal cauldron.

The distant road to the capital was linked with purple mists. He again raised the phrase of medicine and illness treating one another, yet said that he had already been in close reliance for five years.
The seedlings of the śrāmaṇera Weiwei sprout and flourish, their flowers and leaves spreading with ever-increasing fragrance. Yet on Mount Mao,
they are so pungent that even a mere trace turns the blossoms and buds into iron caltrops.

Showing the attendant Lin how to apply a touch of ink as if it were his own long-standing mastery; distinguishing white rice sprinkled with pepper and ginger. As they see each other out the gate, there is nothing said;
beneath the hall, the autumn flowers naturally emit their fragrance.
The thunderous silence upon Huiji’s tongue erupts in a single moment of stillness; though not a mote of dust stirs, he stirs up waves and billows.
Among the countless people at the Flower-Gathering Assembly, none could surpass the *dhūta* monk who broke into a smile.
The novice monk was entrusted with the robe;
at Vulture Peak, what did [the Buddha] entrust to Kāśyapa? Ten times more dense and subtle, yet it turns into something discordant.
At Mount Mao, whether it is thus or not thus, a single thread of an inch-long measure determines its own length.
The Monk Wu seeks words to return to his hermitage;
having traveled east, what did he see that he now returns west? Seeking from me a *gāthā* to point the way for the deluded, may he receive this good news from the head of the hut:
the winter vegetables, after the rain, are lush and green across the rows.
The lamp-master of the minor Buddha-activity hall recognizes the place where the Buddha has gone.
